This is a fascinating and important piece of Sumerian literature. The text you provided is the beginning of the myth known as **"Enki and Ninmah,"** which describes the creation of humankind. The gods are weary from their labor, and they cry out for a solution. This leads the wise god Enki, prompted by his mother Namma, to create humans to take over the gods' toil.

Here is a full translation and breakdown of the text.

***

### Continuous Prose Translation

> From that ancient day, the day when heaven and earth had been created; from that ancient night, the night when heaven and earth had been fashioned; from that ancient year, the year when destinies were decreed; when the Anunna gods were born; when the goddess Inana came to have lordship; when portions were allotted for the goddess Inana in heaven and earth; when the goddess Inana [...] was gloriously born...
>
> In those days, the great gods were overseeing the work, while the lesser gods were bearing the toil. The gods were digging the canals and piling up the silt in Harali. The gods were grinding the clay, and they were setting up a complaint about their lives.
>
s> At that time, the one of wide understanding, the creator, who possessed wisdom in abundance among all the gods—Enki—in the Engur, in the deep, in the inaccessible abyss, a place whose interior no other god had ever seen, was lying on his bed and did not stir from his sleep.
>
> They, the gods, were uttering their lament; they were making a wailing.
>
> To the one who was lying in deep sleep, who was not stirring from his bed, Namma, the primordial mother who gave birth to all the gods, brought the lament of the gods to her son:
>
> "[My son], are you really lying asleep? Are you really slumbering deeply? [From your bed... are you not] stirring? The gods, your own creation, [...] their necks are suffering(?)."

***

### Line-by-Line Translation and Analysis

**1. ud re-a-ta ud an ki-bi-ta ba-an-[dim2-ma-ba]**
*   **Translation:** "From that ancient day, the day when heaven and earth had been created from their place,"
*   **Analysis:** Establishes a mythical, primordial time frame. `ud re-a-ta` means "from that day yonder." The verb `dim2` ("to create/fashion") is reconstructed.

**2. ĝi6 re-a-ta ĝi6 an ki-bi-ta /ba\-[an-dim2-ma-ba]**
*   **Translation:** "From that ancient night, the night when heaven and earth had been created from their place,"
*   **Analysis:** A parallel line to the first, a common feature of Sumerian poetry, emphasizing the antiquity of the events.

**3. [mu re]-a-/ta\ mu nam ba-[tar-ra-ba]**
*   **Translation:** "From that ancient year, the year when destiny was decreed,"
*   **Analysis:** Continues the temporal setting. `nam tar` is the standard term for "to decree fate."

**4. [da]-/nun\-na-ke4-ne ba-tu-ud-da-a-ba**
*   **Translation:** "When the Anunna gods were born,"
*   **Analysis:** The `Anunna` are the major, senior deities in the pantheon. This long series of "when" clauses (temporal clauses ending in `-ba`) sets the scene.

**5. dama-dinana nam-NIR.PA-še3 ba-tuku-a-ba**
*   **Translation:** "When the goddess Inana came to have lordship,"
*   **Analysis:** `dama-dinana` is an unusual writing for Inana, perhaps related to her epithet `ama-ušumgal-ana`. `nam-NIR.PA` likely refers to stewardship or a position of authority.

**6. dama-dinana an ki-a ba-ḫal-ḫal-la-a-ba**
*   **Translation:** "When for the goddess Inana portions were allotted in heaven and earth,"
*   **Analysis:** `ḫal-ḫal` means "to divide portions/shares," referring to the allocation of divine domains and cults.

**7. dama-dinana […] ba-a-peš u3-tud-da-a-ba**
*   **Translation:** "When the goddess Inana […] was gloriously born,"
*   **Analysis:** `u3-tud` = "to give birth/be born." `peš` can mean "to be abundant, to expand," suggesting a magnificent birth. The line is partially damaged.

**8. diĝir kurum6-ma-bi A X X unu2?-bi-še3 ba-ab-keše2-a-<ba>**
*   **Translation:** "When the gods of their food-offerings... for their dwelling place... was prepared,"
*   **Analysis:** This line is heavily damaged and obscure. It seems to refer to the establishment of cults (`kurum6` = food portions/offerings) and temples (`unu2` = dwelling).

**9. diĝir šar2-šar2 kiĝ2-ĝa2 al-sug2-ge-eš diĝir tur-tur du2-lum im-il2-il2-e-ne**
*   **Translation:** "The great gods were overseeing the work, (while) the lesser gods were bearing the toil."
*   **Analysis:** This is the core of the problem. `diĝir šar2-šar2` ("all the gods," i.e., the great gods/Anunna) aresupervising `diĝir tur-tur` ("the small gods," later identified as the Igigi), who must perform the `dulum` (drudgery, corvée labor).

**10. diĝir id2 <im> dun-dun-u3-ne saḫar-bi ḫa-ra-li im-dub-dub-be2-ne**
*   **Translation:** "The gods were digging the canals, piling up its silt in Harali."
*   **Analysis:** Describes the hard labor: `dun` ("to dig") canals and `dub` ("to heap up") the excavated earth (`saḫar`). `Harali` is a mythical, distant land, perhaps here just referring to the piles of earth.

**11. diĝir im ar3-ar3-re-ne zi-bi inim am3-ma-ĝar-re-ne**
*   **Translation:** "The gods were grinding clay, (and) they were setting up a complaint about their lives."
*   **Analysis:** Grinding clay (`im ar3`) was for making bricks. The phrase `inim ... ĝar` ("to place a word") is an idiom for complaining or lodging a protest. `zi-bi` ("their lives") clarifies the subject of their complaint.

**12. ud-ba ĝeštug2 daĝal mud diĝir šar2-šar2 ĝal2-ĝal2**
*   **Translation:** "In those days, the one of wide understanding, the creator, who possessed wisdom in abundance among all the gods—"
*   **Analysis:** This begins a long a series of epithets describing the god Enki. `ĝeštug2 daĝal` ("wide ear/understanding") is his classic attribute.

**13. den-ki-ke4 engur buru3 a-sur-ra ki diĝir na-me šag4-bi u6 nu-um-me**
*   **Translation:** "Enki, in the Engur, in the deep, in the inaccessible abyss, a place whose interior no other god had ever seen,"
*   **Analysis:** Enki's dwelling is the `Engur` (or Apsu), the freshwater abyss. `ki ... u6 nu-um-me` ("a place no-one had seen") emphasizes its mysterious and remote nature.

**14. ki-nu2-ni i3-nu2 u3 ku nu-um-zi-zi**
*   **Translation:** "Was lying on his bed and did not stir from his sleep."
*   **Analysis:** While the gods toil, the god of wisdom is deep in slumber (`u3 ku`), unaware of their plight.

**15. diĝir er2-ra im-pad-pad-ne a-nir ĝal2 i3-ak im-me-ne**
*   **Translation:** "They, the gods, were uttering their lament, they were making a wailing."
*   **Analysis:** The suffering gods cry out. `er2` is a formal "lament," while `a-nir` is a more general "wailing."

**16. lu2 ku-ra i3-nu2-a-ra ki-nu2-bi nu-um-zi-zi-<ra>**
*   **Translation:** "To the one who was lying in deep sleep, who was not stirring from his bed,"
*   **Analysis:** A dative phrase referring to the sleeping Enki. Their lament is directed at him.

**17. dnamma-ke4 ama palil u3-tud diĝir šar2-šar2-ra-ke4-ne**
*   **Translation:** "Namma, the primordial mother who gave birth to all the gods,"
*   **Analysis:** The goddess `Namma`, personification of the primordial sea and mother of Enki, acts as an intermediary. `ama palil` ("first/foremost mother") is her epithet.

**18. er2-ra diĝir-re-e-ne dumu-ni-ir ba-ši-in-de6**
*   **Translation:** "Brought the lament of the gods to her son."
*   **Analysis:** She takes the gods' complaint (`er2-ra`) and brings (`de6`) it to her son, Enki.

**19. X mu-un-ši-nu2-u3-nam u3 mu-un-ši-ku-ku-na-nam**
*   **Translation:** "[My son], are you really lying asleep, are you really slumbering deeply?"
*   **Analysis:** Namma's direct speech to Enki begins. The `X` is likely `dumu-ĝu10` ("my son"). The repetitive phrasing `...-nam ...-nam` conveys her urgency and disbelief.

**20. [X] TE BA [… nu-mu-un]-zi-zi**
*   **Translation:** "[From your bed ... you are not] stirring!"
*   **Analysis:** A broken line that continues her speech, chiding him for his inaction.

**21. dim3-me2-er šu dim2-dim2-ma-zu X gu2?-bi im-tu10-tu10-ne**
*   **Translation:** "The gods, your own creation, [...] their necks are suffering(?)."
*   **Analysis:** `dim3-me2-er` is a variant of `diĝir` (gods). She reminds Enki that the suffering gods are his own handiwork (`šu dim2-ma-zu`). The phrase `gu2...im-tu10-tu10-ne` is obscure; `gu2` is "neck," often associated with bearing burdens. The verb might imply suffering, exhaustion, or growing weak. The translation is conjectural but fits the context.
